note: Theatre parameters and sources. Same discipline as the physiology engine (Milestone 8): every parameter carries a status — cited (traceable to a consulted source below), calibrated (chosen value inside a cited range, disclosed), or verify (engineering placeholder, visibly flagged, never presented as clinical fact). The Rust loader hard-fails any parameter that is neither cited, calibrated, nor verify-flagged, exactly as physiology::Params does.

sources.carries: Primary cause of bile duct injury was a visual perceptual illusion in 97% of cases; technical faults 3%. Stewart-Way classification: class I 7%, class II 22%, class III 61%, class IV 10%. Class III mechanism: the common duct is mistaken for the cystic duct and deliberately transected. Only 25% of injuries were recognised at the index operation.
sources.cite: Way LW, Stewart L, Gantert W, et al. Causes and prevention of laparoscopic bile duct injuries: analysis of 252 cases from a human factors and cognitive psychology perspective. Ann Surg. 2003;237(4):460-469. PMID 12677139.

sources.carries: The three Critical View of Safety criteria: (1) the hepatocystic triangle is cleared of fat and fibrous tissue (the common bile duct and common hepatic duct do not have to be exposed); (2) the lower one-third of the gallbladder is separated from the liver to expose the cystic plate; (3) two and only two structures should be seen entering the gallbladder. The hepatocystic triangle is bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct, and the inferior edge of the liver.
sources.cite: Strasberg SM, Brunt LM. Rationale and use of the critical view of safety in laparoscopic cholecystectomy. J Am Coll Surg. 2010;211(1):132-138 (criteria originally Strasberg et al. 1995).

sources.carries: The critical view of safety is the preferred method of cystic duct identification. A momentary pause to confirm the CVS before clipping or transecting the cystic duct/artery. When the CVS cannot be obtained, the operative strategy should be altered, preferably to subtotal cholecystectomy (laparoscopic or open). Strong recommendations: intraoperative biliary imaging when anatomy is uncertain or injury is suspected; referral of patients with confirmed or suspected bile duct injury to an experienced hepatobiliary surgeon/team.
sources.cite: Brunt LM, Deziel DJ, Telem DA, et al. Safe cholecystectomy multi-society practice guideline and state of the art consensus conference on prevention of bile duct injury during cholecystectomy. Surg Endosc. 2020;34(7):2827-2855. PMID 32399938.

sources.carries: Subtotal cholecystectomy is the bailout when the CVS cannot be attained: it avoids dissecting the hepatocystic triangle. Fenestrating subtype: the gallbladder remnant is left open (no sealed lumen); the cystic duct is closed from inside (e.g. purse-string suture or stapler). Reconstituting subtype: the remnant is closed, reconstituting a lumen in which stones can re-form, with possible need for reoperation.
sources.cite: Strasberg SM, Pucci MJ, Brunt LM, Deziel DJ. Subtotal cholecystectomy — 'fenestrating' vs 'reconstituting' subtypes and the prevention of bile duct injury. J Am Coll Surg. 2016;222(1):89-96.

sources.carries: Cognitive task analysis expanded the laparoscopic cholecystectomy task model from 19 steps (expert recall alone) to 97 microsteps; a 'Step 0: planning the procedure' was added; dissection carried the most microsteps (15) and intraoperative cholangiogram the next most (10). Experts omit 50-70% of steps on unaided recall — the reason this procedure is authored against consulted operative sources, not recalled.
sources.cite: Villarreal ME, et al. Using a task analysis to describe the technical requirements of laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Surg Endosc. 2023;37(5):3921-3925. PMID 37036502.

sources.carries: The three checklist integration points in the procedure model and their phase placement.
sources.cite: World Health Organization. WHO Surgical Safety Checklist. 2008/2009 (19 items, three phases: Sign In before induction of anaesthesia, Time Out before skin incision, Sign Out before the patient leaves the operating room). Outcome data: Haynes AB, et al. A surgical safety checklist to reduce morbidity and mortality in a global population. N Engl J Med. 2009;360:491-499 (death rate 1.5% to 0.8%; inpatient complications 11.0% to 7.0%).

sources.carries: Cefazolin 2 g IV (3 g for patients weighing >=120 kg), started within 60 minutes before surgical incision; redosing interval 4 hours.
sources.cite: Bratzler DW, Dellinger EP, Olsen KM, et al. Clinical practice guidelines for antimicrobial prophylaxis in surgery. Am J Health-Syst Pharm. 2013;70(3):195-283.

sources.carries: GOALS: five domains (depth perception, bimanual dexterity, efficiency, tissue handling, autonomy), each rated 1-5 with descriptive anchors at 1, 3 and 5; total 25. Ships in the procedure's scoring block as rubric data for observed-performance rating; a headless scripted runner cannot populate it (see scoring.notes).
sources.cite: Vassiliou MC, Feldman LS, Andrew CG, et al. A global assessment tool for evaluation of intraoperative laparoscopic skills. Am J Surg. 2005;190(1):107-113.

sources.carries: OSATS global rating scale: seven items (respect for tissue, time and motion, instrument handling, knowledge of instruments, use of assistants, flow of operation, knowledge of specific procedure), each 1-5; total 35. Rubric data only in v1, for the same reason as GOALS.
sources.cite: Martin JA, Regehr G, Reznick R, et al. Objective structured assessment of technical skill (OSATS) for surgical residents. Br J Surg. 1997;84(2):273-276 (global rating items as reproduced in subsequent validation literature).

sources.carries: Debrief structure: Setting the Scene, Reactions, Description, Analysis, Summary. The Analysis phase blends three strategies matched to the performance gap: learner self-assessment (plus-delta), focused facilitation (including advocacy-inquiry), and directive feedback/teaching. The runner's debrief emits Description from the event log, Analysis as plus/delta/directive entries, and a Summary; Setting the Scene and Reactions are facilitator acts in live use and are labelled as such.
sources.cite: Eppich W, Cheng A. Promoting Excellence and Reflective Learning in Simulation (PEARLS): development and rationale for a blended approach to health care simulation debriefing. Simul Healthc. 2015;10(2):106-115. PMID 25710312.

sources.carries: Double cystic artery prevalence 13% (95% CI 11-16%); cystic artery absent in 2% (CI 1-4%); cystic artery origin from the right hepatic artery in 89% (CI 85-92%); mean cystic artery length 20.77 mm, mean diameter 1.91 mm. Basis of the second procedure variant and of the order-of-magnitude anchor for the cystic bleed placeholder.
sources.cite: Asghar K, et al. Double cystic artery: a meta-analysis. Clin Ter. 2024;175(3):184-192. DOI 10.7417/CT.2024.5061. PMID 38767077.

sources.carries: Port placement, retraction directions, window creation, extraction and closure microsteps.
sources.cite: Operative technique references consulted in-session: standard four-port 'American' configuration operative descriptions (10 mm infraumbilical camera port; 10 mm epigastric port placed about 2 cm below the liver edge to the right of the falciform ligament; 5 mm mid-clavicular and 5 mm anterior-axillary working ports; fundus retracted cephalad over the liver dome; infundibulum retracted caudolaterally; windows created between cystic duct and cystic artery and between cystic artery and liver edge before division; specimen extracted in a retrieval bag via the umbilical port; fascial closure at 10 mm port sites).

sources.carries: Surgical treatment and peri-operative antibiotics for acute appendicitis. A single preoperative dose of broad-spectrum antibiotics is recommended in patients undergoing appendectomy; postoperative antibiotics are recommended against in uncomplicated appendicitis and should not be prolonged beyond 3-5 days in complicated appendicitis with adequate source control. Recommendation 4.8 (strong, 1B): peritoneal irrigation has no advantage over suction alone in complicated appendicitis; perform suction alone. Statement 4.12: in adults, drains after appendectomy for perforated appendicitis should be discouraged - no benefit in preventing intra-abdominal abscess, longer hospitalisation, low-quality evidence of increased 30-day morbidity/mortality. Stump closure: endoloops/suture ligation or polymeric clips recommended for uncomplicated and complicated appendicitis; endostaplers may be used in complicated cases depending on the intra-operative judgement of the surgeon; simple ligation is recommended over stump inversion (1A). Intra-operative grading of appendicitis is recommended.
sources.cite: Di Saverio S, Podda M, De Simone B, et al. Diagnosis and treatment of acute appendicitis: 2020 update of the WSES Jerusalem guidelines. World J Emerg Surg. 2020;15:27. DOI 10.1186/s13017-020-00306-3.

sources.carries: Systematic review/meta-analysis of appendicitis management. KQ5: no significant differences in outcomes of complicated appendicitis between suction only and suction plus lavage. KQ6: in children undergoing appendectomy for complicated appendicitis, drains placed at operation were associated with higher risk of reoperation (RR 2.04); in adults no significant difference between drain and no-drain groups was found. Dual source with T14 for the suction and drain rubrics (the guideline recommends; the meta-analysis quantifies).
sources.cite: SAGES. Diagnosis and Treatment of Appendicitis: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Society of American Gastrointestinal and Endoscopic Surgeons guideline publication, consulted in-session at sages.org.

sources.carries: Positions of the vermiform appendix in 377 dissected adult cadavers: retrocecal 43.5%, subcecal 24.4%, post-ileal 14.3%, pelvic 9.3%, paracecal 5.8%, pre-ileal 2.4%, other 0.27%; mean length 11.4 cm. The same review reports Wakeley's analysis of 10,000 cases: retrocecal/retrocolic 65.28%, pelvic 31.01%, subcecal 2.26%, pre-ileal 1.0%, post-ileal 0.4%. Basis of the appendicectomy variant prevalences.
sources.cite: de Souza SC, da Costa SRM, de Souza IGS. Vermiform appendix: positions and length - a study of 377 cases and literature review. J Coloproctol (Rio J). 2015;35(4):212-216. DOI 10.1016/j.jcol.2015.08.003.

sources.carries: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials of appendix stump closure (8 RCTs, 850 participants): no differences in total, intraoperative or postoperative complications between ligature (endoloop/Roeder loop/knot) and mechanical closure (stapler, clips, electrothermal) for uncomplicated appendicitis; mechanical devices saved about nine minutes of operating time; the evidence is of very low quality throughout, so no superiority claim is made for either family - the base-condition rule in the procedure model rests on T14 and T18, not on this review.
sources.cite: Closure methods of the appendix stump for complications during laparoscopic appendectomy. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (searches to June 2017), consulted in-session.

sources.carries: 242 children undergoing laparoscopic appendectomy: no stump leaks with either endoloop or endostapler closure; in perforated appendicitis intra-abdominal abscess was more frequent in the endostapler group, which the authors attribute to the quality of the appendiceal stump rather than the closure technique; two of the three surgeons used the endoloop routinely UNLESS the condition of the appendiceal base favoured the endostapler to ensure sealing of healthy tissue - the practice the procedure model's closure rule scores. Costs favoured the endoloop ($57 vs $251 per case in disposables).
sources.cite: Endoloop versus endostapler closure of the appendiceal stump in pediatric laparoscopic appendectomy. Can J Surg. 2012;55(1):37-40. DOI 10.1503/cjs.023810.

sources.carries: Operative descriptions consulted in-session: three-port laparoscopic appendectomy - 10-12 mm umbilical port by open cutdown or Veress, pneumoperitoneum to a maximum of 15 mmHg, 5 mm ports in the left lower quadrant and the suprapubic midline (bladder care at the suprapubic site); grasp the appendix and follow the taeniae coli down to their confluence at the base of the cecum. SCORE-curriculum chapter: patient position and monitors set for right-lower-quadrant access; the cecum is confirmed by its taeniae and paler colour; the appendix is located by seeking the convergence of the taeniae, the appendix's longitudinal muscle being the continuation of the three taeniae; a window is created in the mesoappendix at the base; the appendix is divided with a stapler gastrointestinal load and the mesentery with a vascular load in the stapler variant of the operation; a large or contaminated appendix is removed in a retrieval bag; trocar sites above 5 mm are closed; the chapter's operation includes mobilization of the right colon for a retrocecal appendix.
sources.cite: Operative technique references consulted in-session: laparoscopic appendectomy operative chapters (three-port technique; SCORE - Surgical Council on Resident Education - laparoscopic appendectomy and Meckel diverticulum chapter, 'ESSENTIAL COMMON' procedure).

sources.carries: Appendicectomy module's in-repo anchors: design/05-theatre.md (procedure format, safety-gate semantics - a gate must be achieved AND demonstrated before dependent steps unlock, dividing an unidentified critical structure fails the attempt; variant gate >=1% prevalence plus injury consequence; bailouts score positively). Milestone 11 digestive records: dig.cecum-appendix is a compound clinical record ('Cecum and appendix'; its TA2 note records the pair has no single TA2 term) whose geometry records are canal.appendix and canal.cecum in data/digestive/digestive-inventory.json, with peritoneum.mesoappendix and the colon.taenia-* records in the same inventory. Milestone 5 cardiovascular inventory: artery.appendicular-artery (appendicular artery) exists as an inventory record in data/cardiovascular/cv-inventory.json but has no clinical record in data/cardiovascular/cardiovascular.json - stated as such in the procedure's register.
sources.cite: Project sources consulted in-repo: design/05-theatre.md; Milestone 11 digestive module records; Milestone 5 cardiovascular inventory.

sources.carries: The operation's step sequence: setup and anesthesia, skin incision, palmar fascia incision, transverse carpal ligament release, carpal tunnel inspection, closure. Standard open incision: longitudinal, from Kaplan's cardinal line distally to the distal wrist crease proximally, along the axis of the radial border of the ring finger, 3-5 mm ulnar to the thenar crease, approximately 3-4 cm. The transverse carpal ligament must be clearly visible and exposed before division, to avoid injuring an intraligamentous variation of the recurrent motor branch; a small opening is made with a scalpel or beaver blade and the ligament is divided longitudinally near its ulnar aspect, directed toward the ring finger, away from the recurrent branch. Distal extension runs until the volar fat pad around the superficial palmar arch is encountered - the landmark that the ligament has been released completely; proximally the antebrachial fascia is released approximately 2.5 cm proximal to the wrist crease on the ulnar side of the palmaris longus. Completeness is checked by sliding a smooth instrument such as a Freer elevator alongside the nerve to ensure it is free proximally and distally; an intraligamentous recurrent branch, when found, is carefully released from the ligament. Internal neurolysis, epineurotomy and tenosynovectomy are rarely indicated and are not a routine part of primary release. Elective carpal tunnel surgery does not require local or systemic antibiotics: multicentre studies of elective soft-tissue hand surgery and of elective carpal tunnel surgery specifically show no statistical difference in infection rates with or without preoperative antibiotics, including in diabetic patients. Lanz groups as reproduced there: group II accessory branches at the distal tunnel 7.2%, group III high division 2.8%, group IV accessory branches proximal to the tunnel 1.6%; the extraligamentous course is found in 80-90% of cases in the later studies the chapter cites.
sources.cite: Open Techniques for Carpal Tunnel Release. In: Green's Operative Hand Surgery (operative hand surgery textbook chapter), consulted in full text in-session.

sources.carries: The carpal tunnel runs from Kaplan's cardinal line distally to the wrist flexion crease proximally. The superficial palmar arch lies typically 18 mm distal to the distal edge of the transverse carpal ligament - the distal limit of safe division. The ligament attaches to the scaphoid and trapezium radially and to the pisiform and hook of the hamate ulnarly. Approaching the ligament at its ulnar border maintains greater distance from the recurrent motor branch and protects it; the branch pierces the ligament (transligamentous) in approximately 20% of the series the chapter cites. The palmar cutaneous branch arises approximately 5-6 cm proximal to the wrist flexion crease and runs along the ulnar aspect of the flexor carpi radialis; injury to it is avoided by staying ulnar and dividing the antebrachial fascia under direct vision. Bright yellow fat at the distal end of the ligament denotes that dissection has gone far enough distally and warns of the nearby palmar arch.
sources.cite: Palmar Approaches (surgical exposures of the hand and wrist). In: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, consulted in full text in-session.

sources.carries: The classification of median nerve variations in the carpal tunnel, from 246 operated carpal tunnels reporting 29 variations: group I, variations in the course of the thenar (recurrent motor) branch - extraligamentous, subligamentous, transligamentous; group II, accessory branches at the distal part of the tunnel; group III, high division of the median nerve; group IV, accessory branches proximal to the tunnel. Bibliographic record and group structure as given in T21, T22 and the classification literature consulted in-session.
sources.cite: Lanz U. Anatomical variations of the median nerve in the carpal tunnel. J Hand Surg Am. 1977;2(1):44-53.

sources.carries: Pooled course prevalences for the recurrent motor branch of the median nerve: extraligamentous 75.2%, subligamentous 13.5%, transligamentous 11.3%. The transligamentous figure is the prevalence carried by variant.transligamentous-recurrent-branch (variant gate: >= 1%).
sources.cite: Henry BM, et al. Meta-analysis of the anatomical variations of the median nerve in the carpal tunnel (31 studies, 3,918 hands), 2015; pooled prevalences as summarised in the Lanz classification reference consulted in-session.

sources.carries: A bifid median nerve was observed in 15 of 160 wrists (9.4%) and a persistent median artery in 12 of 160 (7.5%); the two coexisted in 10 (6.3%), a coexistence more probable than either variant alone (bifid only 3.1%, artery only 1.3%). The persistent median artery figure is the prevalence carried by variant.persistent-median-artery (Lanz group III: high division of the nerve, with the artery between its trunks).
sources.cite: Sonographic findings of the bifid median nerve and persistent median artery in carpal tunnel: a preliminary study in Chinese individuals. Clinics (Sao Paulo); 160 wrists examined by ultrasound with colour Doppler, consulted in-session.

sources.carries: Multicentre retrospective review of 3,003 carpal tunnel releases: 11 surgical site infections overall; antibiotic use did not decrease the risk of infection, including in the 546 patients with diabetes. The authors' conclusion: the routine use of antibiotic prophylaxis in carpal tunnel release surgery is not indicated. Dual source with T21's statement and T28's recommendation for this procedure's no-prophylaxis process design.
sources.cite: Harness NG, Inacio MC, Pfeil FP, Paxton LW. Rate of infection after carpal tunnel release surgery and effect of antibiotic prophylaxis. J Hand Surg Am. 2010;35(2):189-196.

sources.carries: Open carpal tunnel release remains the gold standard procedure. The most common reason for persistent symptoms after carpal tunnel release is the incomplete release of the transverse carpal ligament, occurring distally at the palmar arch or proximally at the volar forearm antebrachial fascia, and attributed to inadequate exposure and visualization. Iatrogenic injury at release can involve the palmar cutaneous nerve (injury avoidable with a more ulnarly positioned incision), the digital nerves, and the median and ulnar nerves themselves. Revision rate 1.5% in 7,464 releases (Westenberg et al. 2020, as reviewed there), with endoscopic release among the risk factors for revision.
sources.cite: Revision of carpal tunnel surgery. J Clin Med. 2022 (Roth|McFarlane Hand and Upper Limb Centre / Washington University review), consulted in full text in-session.

sources.carries: Surgery is the most effective long-term treatment for carpal tunnel syndrome; release is offered for persistent troublesome symptoms, denervation or thenar weakness. Strong evidence: no difference in patient-reported outcomes between mini-open and endoscopic carpal tunnel release. Limited evidence: perioperative prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated for the prevention of surgical site infection following carpal tunnel release. Local anaesthetic alone can be used for the release. Postoperative supervised therapy is not routinely prescribed.
sources.cite: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons. Management of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: evidence-based clinical practice guideline. Adopted May 2024. Summary: Shapiro LM, Kamal RN, et al. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2025;33(7):e356-e366. (The same guideline the case module consulted as its source C24 at Milestone 41.)

sources.carries: In-situ (open) decompression: a single longitudinal incision over the cubital tunnel with visual exposure several centimetres proximally and distally; the ulnar nerve can be compressed at several sites, from as far proximally as the arcade of Struthers, down through the cubital tunnel, to the distal Osborne's ligament, and the open approach lets the surgeon ensure freedom of movement along the entire course of the nerve. Complications of open decompression are generally low: most frequently incisional tenderness and numbness in the distribution of the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve; incision length is often 8-10 cm or more, which poses a substantial threat of injury to that nerve. Subcutaneous anterior transposition: additional subcutaneous dissection anterior to the medial epicondyle forms a bed for the nerve, and a sling created from the underlying muscle fascia and attached to the dermis retains it in its transposed position. Comparative outcomes across all techniques: no technique has demonstrated universal superiority; a meta-analysis by Chen et al. found outcomes equivalent between subcutaneous transposition and in-situ decompression (p = 0.891) with a significantly higher complication rate for transposition (p = 0.05). The review's stated consensus: transposition is preferred where the ulnar nerve tends to subluxate on preoperative or intraoperative examination — stated together with its evidence caveat: beyond one comparative study's subluxation subgroup (Bimmler), there appear to be no studies comparing in-situ decompression against transposition in that subset, and there is little evidence supporting the preference beyond biomechanical logic.
sources.cite: Surgical Approaches and Their Outcomes in the Treatment of Cubital Tunnel Syndrome. Front Surg. 2018;5:48. DOI 10.3389/fsurg.2018.00048. Consulted in full text in-session.

sources.carries: Meta-analysis of the four randomised controlled trials comparing simple decompression with anterior transposition of the ulnar nerve (two submuscular, two subcutaneous): no significant differences in clinical outcome scores (standardised mean difference -0.04, 95% CI -0.36 to 0.28, p = 0.81; three studies, 261 patients) or in postoperative motor nerve-conduction velocities (SMD 0.24, 95% CI -0.15 to 0.63 in favour of simple decompression, p = 0.23; two reports, 100 patients). The confidence intervals are narrow and probably exclude clinically meaningful differences; in patients without prior elbow trauma or surgery, simple decompression is a reasonable alternative to transposition. The randomised-evidence basis of this procedure's equipoise statement.
sources.cite: Zlowodzki M, Chan S, Bhandari M, Kalliainen L, Schubert W. Anterior transposition compared with simple decompression for treatment of cubital tunnel syndrome: a meta-analysis of randomized, controlled trials. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2007. Abstract consulted in-session.

sources.carries: Single-surgeon retrospective cohort, 2010-2023 (open in-situ decompression n=19, endoscopic decompression n=37, minimum 24 months' follow-up), whose operative protocol implements the stability rule this procedure encodes: following complete decompression, ulnar nerve stability is dynamically assessed throughout full elbow flexion and extension; patients with intraoperative instability or subluxation undergo anterior transposition, whereas decompression alone is performed when nerve stability is preserved. In-situ technique: a longitudinal incision along the course of the nerve between the medial epicondyle and the olecranon; the nerve is identified and decompressed proximally and distally, including release of the Osborne ligament and other compressive fascial structures; when present, an arcade of Struthers is also released as part of the proximal decompression; distal decompression continues through the aponeurotic band between the humeral and ulnar heads of flexor carpi ulnaris until the motor branches are visualised. Open anterior submuscular transposition: the nerve is mobilised sufficiently in both directions while preserving the perineural vascular structures, the proximal release is extended to the arcade of Struthers, a submuscular bed is created within the common flexor muscle mass anterior to the medial epicondyle, the nerve is transposed without tension, and the elbow is taken through a full range of flexion and extension to confirm unrestricted gliding and the absence of residual tension; in the endoscopic-assisted transposition, the medial intermuscular septum is released proximally under direct visualisation and a medially based fascial sling created from the fascia of the common flexor mass retains the transposed nerve. All procedures under brachial plexus block anaesthesia with a pneumatic tourniquet, patient supine; active elbow range-of-motion exercises begin on postoperative day 3 in all patients, and after submuscular transposition forceful gripping is avoided for approximately three weeks. One patient in the open decompression group developed a medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve injury. No significant differences in functional outcomes between the open and endoscopic decompression groups.
sources.cite: Open and endoscopic decompression for cubital tunnel syndrome: long-term clinical outcomes, prognostic factors, and comparison of anterior transposition techniques. Arch Orthop Trauma Surg. 2026. DOI 10.1007/s00402-026-06548-1. Consulted in full text in-session.

sources.carries: Recurring luxation of the ulnar nerve at the elbow is not uncommon (16.2%), occurring about equally in young and old, male and female, athletes and non-athletes, with greater mobility usually at the dominant arm; the probable cause is congenital laxity of the supporting ligaments. Subluxating nerves that stop on the tip of the medial epicondyle at 90 degrees or more of flexion are more subject to direct trauma than completely displaced nerves. The 16.2% figure is the prevalence carried by variant.subluxating-nerve (variant gate: >= 1%): it is a general-population anatomical prevalence of recurrent luxation, not a measured frequency of instability found at operation after release, and the register entry says so.
sources.cite: Childress HM. Recurrent ulnar-nerve dislocation at the elbow. Clin Orthop Relat Res. 1975;(108):168-173. PMID 1139823. Abstract consulted in-session.

sources.carries: Retrospective review of 919 cubital tunnel operations (in-situ decompression, subcutaneous transposition and submuscular transposition) at a tertiary care centre: surgical site infection in 5 of 296 patients (1.7%) who received no preoperative antibiotics and 17 of 623 (2.7%) who did; preoperative antibiotics produced no significant change in infection rate (odds ratio 95% CI 0.597-1.633), regardless of patient comorbidities. The authors' conclusion: preoperative antibiotics do not demonstrate benefit for patients undergoing uncomplicated ulnar nerve releases at the elbow (level 4 evidence, retrospective). The elbow-specific source for this procedure's no-prophylaxis process design: the literature behind the Milestone 42 position covered clean soft-tissue procedures of the hand, wrist and forearm, and this study fills the elbow gap those sources left.
sources.cite: Zheng A, Fowler JR. The effectiveness of preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis in ulnar nerve release at the cubital tunnel. Hand (N Y). 2024. DOI 10.1177/15589447221107688. Abstract consulted in-session.

sources.carries: Failure after ulnar nerve decompression at the elbow is defined as no change in the patient's symptoms, or an initial improvement with recurrence. Its causes are classified as diagnostic (incorrect or coexistent diagnoses), TECHNICAL — incomplete decompression, creation of a new area of compression or subluxation, or injury to the cutaneous or ulnar nerves — or biologic (perineural fibrosis, significant preoperative nerve damage). Technical errors and perineural fibrosis necessitate revision surgery; no one procedure is superior in the revision setting as long as a complete decompression is achieved from the arcade of Struthers to the flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) and flexor/pronator aponeurosis, with a compression-free, stable transposition of the surgeon's choice. The failure taxonomy behind this procedure's computed consequences: incomplete release, new compression site, unaddressed subluxation/instability, and injury to the ulnar or medial antebrachial cutaneous nerves are the specialty's own named technical failures of this operation.
sources.cite: Evaluation and Treatment of Failed Ulnar Nerve Release at the Elbow. Orthop Clin North Am. 2012;43(4):487-494. DOI 10.1016/j.ocl.2012.07.018. Key points and chapter text consulted in-session.

sources.carries: Revision surgery for 21 failed subcutaneous transpositions of the ulnar nerve (2001-2019, minimum two years' follow-up): intraoperative findings revealed proximal compression at the arcade of Struthers in 71.4% of patients, distal compression at the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis in 38%, and an intact medial intermuscular septum in 76.2%. The authors' conclusion: inadequate decompression at key anatomical sites — the arcade of Struthers, the medial intermuscular septum and the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis — significantly contributes to the failure of subcutaneous nerve transposition. The quantitative basis for this procedure's release-extent discipline and for the medial intermuscular septum step in the transposition configuration.
sources.cite: Outcomes and intraoperative findings of revision surgery for failed subcutaneous transposition of the ulnar nerve. JSES Int. 2025;9:893-901 (article S2666-6383(25)00025-8). Abstract and results text consulted in-session.

sources.carries: Chapter 12 fixation rule: in TEP and TAPP inguinal/femoral hernia repair non-fixation of mesh is recommended in almost all hernia types except large medial defects (M3 EHS classification) where mesh fixation is recommended; atraumatic fixation (fibrin glue, cyanoacrylate) should be considered to minimise acute postoperative pain; fixation methods listed: tacks, staples, self-fixing, fibrin sealants, glues and sutures; consensus does not exist about a 'best' fixation method. Chapter 18: vascular injuries at dissection and mesh fixation or suturing in the preperitoneal space typically involve the epigastric vessels or the aberrant obturator vessels crossing Cooper's ligament, the so-called corona mortis; mesh exposed to the abdominal cavity through peritoneal defects may cause bowel adhesions resulting in bowel obstruction; fixation complications include mesh migration, adhesions, erosion, recurrence, 'meshoma', tack hernias and chronic pain. Antibiotic prophylaxis is never recommended in laparo-endoscopic repair. Clinically significant chronic postoperative inguinal pain incidence 10-12%.
sources.cite: HerniaSurge Group. International guidelines for groin hernia management. Hernia. 2018;22(1):1-165. DOI 10.1007/s10029-017-1668-x. PMC5809582. PMID 29330835.

sources.carries: Antibiotic prophylaxis is not suggested in elective laparo-endoscopic inguinal hernia repair in any patient and in any risk environment (weak recommendation). A heavyweight mesh is recommended, especially in a large and direct hernia, to reduce recurrence (strong); light-weight mesh thresholds <50 g/m2, heavyweight >70 g/m2; recurrence was increased after lightweight mesh especially in non-fixated mesh used in direct inguinal hernia repairs (RR 7.27, Bakker et al. meta-analysis as reported). Trial sequential analysis showed data still insufficient concerning mesh fixation - the fixation chapter was not among the ten updated. Occult hernia chapter: exploration with TEP requires direct dissection of the myopectineal orifice; TAPP exploration has limitations in the recognition of small defects and cord lipomas.
sources.cite: Stabilini C, et al. Update of the international HerniaSurge guidelines for groin hernia management. BJS Open. 2023;7(5):zrad080. DOI 10.1093/bjsopen/zrad080.

sources.carries: The critical view of the myopectineal orifice (Daes & Felix 2017) and the inverted Y with five triangles (Furtado et al. 2019): inverted Y = inferior epigastric vessels superiorly, vas deferens medially, spermatic vessels laterally, iliopubic tract horizontal through the deep ring. Gating sentence: 'Only if all anatomical elements have been recognized, the steps of dissection described above have been completed and hemostasis achieved should the surgeon proceed with mesh placement.' Rule 1: TAPP peritoneal incision at least 4 cm above the deep ring, from the ASIS to the medial umbilical fold. Rule 2: the nerves should not be systematically dissected or identified as is recommended in open repairs. Rule 5: parietalization is sufficient when the peritoneum is dissected inferiorly until the vas deferens crosses the external iliac vein and the iliopsoas is identified posteriorly. Rule 6: large/inguinoscrotal sacs are transected and the distal sac abandoned, and sac transection is done only after safely identifying the elements of the spermatic cord. Rule 7: cord lipoma is explored and reduced - a major cause of recurrence. Rule 8: mesh usually at least 10 cm craniocaudal x 15 cm mediolateral, covering the myopectineal orifice with overlap at least 3-4 cm. Rule 9: mesh fixation is unnecessary in most MIS inguinal hernia repairs and is recommended in large inguinal hernias, especially direct (M3 EHS); traumatic fixation should not be placed below the iliopubic tract - consider 2 cm above the iliopubic tract for extra safety to avoid injury in the triangles of pain or doom; 5-6 fixation points are sufficient and higher tack numbers are associated with increased risk of chronic pain. Rule 10: TAPP peritoneal closure by suture is recommended instead of tacking; most surgeons agree gaps, holes or tears of the peritoneum should be closed to reduce the risk of early bowel obstruction or mesh exposure.
sources.cite: Claus C, Furtado M, Malcher F, Cavazzola LT, Felix E. Ten golden rules for a safe MIS inguinal hernia repair. Surg Endosc. 2020;34(4):1458-1464. DOI 10.1007/s00464-020-07449-z. Consulted in full text in-session.

sources.carries: The triangle of doom: 'the dangerous triangle (the triangle of doom) refers to a triangular area bound by the vas deferens, the testicular vessels and the peritoneal fold. Within the boundaries of this area, you can find the external iliac artery and vein.' The triangle of pain: 'a triangular area located lateral to the dangerous triangle and bound by the iliopubic tract, the testicular vessels and the peritoneal fold. This area from lateral to medial includes the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, the femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve and the femoral nerve'; the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve and the femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve are more commonly damaged; those nerves can suffer major damage or entrapment when performing separation or fixation or when controlling bleeding, which may cause chronic neuropathic pain. Corona mortis: anastomotic vessels between the inferior epigastric or external iliac vessels and the obturator arteries or veins, visualised about 5 cm from the pubic symphysis arching over Cooper's ligament; significant haemorrhage may occur and haemostasis may be difficult if they are accidentally cut because they may retract into the obturator canal. Cooper's ligament is a structure that can hold a mesh and tacks. The lateral part of a mesh should be fixated just above the level of the iliopubic tract. The vas deferens/round ligament and testicular vessels can be completely exposed only when the internal spermatic fascia is incised and the hernia sac separated cephalad.
sources.cite: Yang XF, Liu JL. Anatomy essentials for laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair. Ann Transl Med. 2016;4(19):372. DOI 10.21037/atm.2016.09.32. PMC5075841. PMID 27826575. Consulted in full text in-session.

sources.carries: Corona mortis was found present in nearly half of the general population (49.3%), with venous corona mortis (41.7%) more common than arterial (17.0%); pooled mean arterial corona mortis distance from the pubic symphysis 59.90 mm. The 49.3% figure is the prevalence carried by variant.corona-mortis (variant gate: >= 1%): any corona mortis connection (anastomosis between the obturator system and the external iliac or inferior epigastric vessels behind the superior pubic ramus), arterial or venous.
sources.cite: Sanna A, et al. Corona mortis meta-analysis. Injury. 2018;49:302-308. DOI 10.1016/j.injury.2017.12.007 - as reported in Konarska-Wlosinska M, et al. Exploring the topography of the obturator artery and corona mortis. Int Urogynecol J. 2024. PMC11150310. PMID 38635039. Consulted in full text in-session.

sources.carries: 'From 2 per cent to 5 per cent of all indirect inguinal hernias are of the sliding variety. (Sliding hernias are those in which part of the wall of the sac is formed by a viscus.)' The proportion is even higher in the aged; found almost exclusively in males and usually on the left side. The 2-5% figure is the prevalence carried by variant.sliding-hernia (variant gate: >= 1%).
sources.cite: Gaspar MR, Woolley MM, Joergenson EJ. Sliding indirect inguinal hernia. Calif Med. 1956;85(5):330-334. PMC1532016. PMID 13364683. Abstract consulted in-session.
